interpretations.text: The finite-budget native search reduced the dimensionless signed maximum excess from 20.451754937763166 at baseline to 14.977470268699308, an absolute reduction of 5.474284669063858 within this sampled-model comparison. Holding maximum speed decreased from 0.4290350987552633 m/s to 0.31377399454640326 m/s, while holding maximum position error increased from 0.12531739147659965 m to 0.1597747026869931 m. Consequently, the worst sampled constraint changed from holding speed to holding position. The best candidate still failed the holding-position limit of 0.01 m: its value was 0.1597747026869931 m at 0.45 s, corresponding to normalized signed excess 14.977470268699308. Thus, no passing control was found under the recorded initialization, 12-dimensional parameterization, tension bounds of 0–8 N, and finite search budget.

The search stopped at its iteration limit after 84 optimization evaluations and 84 native rollouts totaling 84,000 physics steps; convergence and global optimality were not established. The observed failure therefore does not prove global nonlinear infeasibility, structural infeasibility, or absence of a passing control under another parameterization or search trajectory. Task acceptance also remains unmeasured: these are sampled native-model diagnostics over 0–0.5 s, not evidence of continuous-time compliance, hardware performance, robustness, repeatability, or an independently accepted task pass. The opposing changes in speed and position error show a trade-off in the returned candidate, but they do not identify its physical cause.

Discriminating evidence is still missing: an applicable independent full-duration replay and frozen task-acceptance evaluation of the recorded control schedule are required to determine whether the candidate satisfies the actual task. Additional evidence would also be needed to distinguish a genuine capability limitation from finite optimization budget, solver convergence, or control-parameterization limitations. No such physical acceptance or broader-search evidence is present in this Study.

The completed physical replay was a valid task failure. Terminal position error was 0.15160971560597297 m against a 0.01 m limit; holding maximum position error was 0.1597747026869931 m against 0.01 m; and holding maximum speed was 0.31377399454640326 m/s against 0.02 m/s. Their authoritative normalized signed excesses were 14.160971560597297, 14.977470268699308, and 14.688699727320163, respectively, making holding position the dominant reported constraint. Force-bound violation was exactly 0.0 N and passed its 1e-08 N limit, while solver errors were exactly 0 and passed the zero-error requirement. Thus, the failure reflects observed task-performance violations, not an invalid evaluation, force-limit violation, or recorded solver failure.

Persistent motion during the holding interval is directly consistent with the holding-speed failure. At 0.45 s, speed reached the reported maximum of 0.31377399454640326 m/s, with tip velocity [0.13663442641150733, -0.12674784551758458, 0.2524284786418823] m/s. At 0.50 s, speed had fallen to 0.08759627668448378 m/s but remained 0.06759627668448378 m/s above the 0.02 m/s limit. This supports the limited explanation that the tip had not settled sufficiently by the end of the replay. However, it does not identify the mechanical or control cause: no diagnostic relations or recorded control diagnostics are available, and changing tendon tensions alone cannot establish causation.

The evidence cannot determine whether the failure arose from controller design, model mismatch, transient timing, tendon actuation behavior, or another mechanism. Position error is unavailable in the two cited samples, so those instantaneous records cannot localize when the maximum holding-position error occurred or relate it directly to the observed velocities. With only one physical launch and no mathematical reintegrations, NMPC updates, or RL actions, repeatability and comparative improvement are also unresolved. Time-resolved target and position error, controller commands and diagnostics, relevant state histories, and repeated comparable executions would be needed to discriminate among mechanisms; the current replay cannot establish feasibility, infeasibility, robustness, continuous-time compliance, or hardware performance.
